content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a method to finetune a predtrained text to image diffusion model to match the data statistics of a new dataset. They propose to do this by first optimizing a text embedding that represents the new dataset and initialize the reverse process of diffusion using statistics of the dataset learnt using a VAE. Results are shown on several datasets and state of the art performance is demonstrated over stable diffusion.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths:

1. **Writing quality:**  The paper is well written with great attention to detail. All the necessary design steps are adequately motivated. 

2. **Simplicity:** The proposed approach is simple and elegant. Particularly, it mostly involves optimization on the text embedding space and smart initialization for the reverse diffusion process. 

3. **Insights:** The paper provide important insights on what changes can be made to a standard large text to image diffusion model to adapt it to new datasets. The proposed approach is general enough that in theory can also be applied to other large diffusion models. 

4. **Reproducibility:** The simplicity of the approach coupled with the detailed explanation of the various design elements leads to ease of reproducibility. 

5. **Experimental analysis:** Results are provided on variety of datasets (both in terms of scale and content) to demonstrate the generalizability of the approach.  

## Weaknesses 

1. **Technical Novelty:** The technical novelty is somewhat limited as the textual inversion idea borrows from Gal et al. and the smart initialization is a side effect of the original stable diffusion pipeline. That being said, although the approach borrows ideas from existing works, the insights provided are helpful in using these diffusion models in a wider variety of use cases.

2. **Quantitative Analysis:** Additional quantitative analysis, primarily regarding consistence of the generated image to text prompt would be helpful. 

3. **Ablations:** No ablations are provided with regards to qualitative/ quantitative performance without the smart noise initialization or without the textual inversion based fine tuning of text embedding. Reporting a small ablation study of this kind (on atleast one of the dataset) would be very instructive with respect to which component makes the most difference in adapting these frameworks to a new dataset. 

4. **Metrics:** It is possible that the method is over engineered to produce good KID scores whilst not actually improving consistency to target distribution (although it doesn't appear so). Although not *strictly* necessary, it is nonetheless beneficial to report additional metrics like FID, or mean LPIPS deviation for model trained with/ without the proposed approach, to further highlight the improvements.

5. **Controllability:** It is unclear if the model loses the ability to generate text controlled images after the fine tuning step (as it appears that the text conditioning has been marginalized out for the target dataset). Is it possible to still maintain text based generation on the target dataset? Is the limitation due to the fact that we do not have text annotations for the target dataset?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity:** The paper is well written with all details explained adequately. All the design components are sufficiently motivated and the narrative is clear with regards to what the framework sets out to achieve.

**Quality:** The quality of the writing and the results are adequate. Although, the work would benefit from additional quantitative analysis and some ablations

**Novelty:** The technical novelty is somewhat limited since every step uses ideas from previous works, however, the framework as a whole would serve as a strong baseline for any future approach that will explore the problem of adapting large text-to-image diffusion models to different use cases. 

**Reproducibility:** The framework is fairly simple and should be easy to reimplement. However, no code is provided which would make it harder to reproduce the exact numbers presented in the manuscript.
content.summary_of_the_review: The authors present a simple and elegant framework for adapting a text-to-image model to a custom dataset. Although the method is interesting and provides valuable insights, I think the work would benefit from additional quantitative evaluation and especially ablations. I am mostly positive about the framework, however I am willing to raise my scores if the authors are able to address some of the above mentioned comments.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This work uses textual inversion from Gal et al. (2022) + an informative prior to get a prompt which is representative of a users dataset. They then use this prompt to generate more images in that same distribution. They claim this is significantly better than just using a non-finetuned stable diffusion, while being cheaper to compute than stable diffusion at inference time.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
#### Strengths

- The qualitative results look good.
- Writing quality is excellent.
- The idea is straightforward and effective.

#### Weaknesses

- Can the authors clarify in what significant way this method differs from textural inversion? As is, the novelty seems limited.
- It doesn't show that these new generated datasets have a utility. Further, to optimize the text prompt embedding, you still need to backprop through the entire diffusion model, so this doesn't make it easier to optimize in VRAM limited environments (the author's motivating example).
- The improvements in sampling speed are pretty marginal, and given that the optimal stopping time is found wrt a quantitative metric (which can be flaky for small differences in value) its unclear if this is actually significant.
- Fundamentally, textual inversion is a lightweight finetuning method. Any use of textual inversion like this needs comparison to other lightweight finetuning methods.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Clarity**

The paper is clear and easy to understand.

**Novelty**

The novelty is limited. It doesn't seem to add significantly to the original textural inversion paper (Gal et al. 2022).

**Quality**

Writing quality is good. Experiments are not thorough enough for an empirical work.

**Reproducibility**

Reproducibility seems good.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Diffusion model for Your Own Data (DYOD) as a framework to customize a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model on customized small datasets. The proposed method uses textual-inversion to get a special token to represent the personalized dataset, and then uses SDEdit to control the geometry of samples, where the denoising process is initialized from VAE outputs. The proposed method is evaluated on five datasets: Nike-shoes, Apple-orange, Lego-face, Simpsons-faces, and Brain MRI.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## strengths
- The problem of customizing and personalizing pre-trained diffusion models is of great interest to the community. The proposed DYOD framework shows promising results on datasets like Lego-face, Simpsons-faces, and Brain MRI.
- The proposed method is simple and suggests a promising technique to initialize the sampling process.
## weakness
- Some parts of the paper seem a bit misleading and unclear. For the diffusion model part of the proposed method, is StableDiffusion used? If so, naming the baseline as “Stable Diffusion” is misleading. I guess it is better to call it “textual-inversion” as the main purpose is to compare DYOD with textual-inversion?
- The proposed method seems to be a simple combination of Textual-Inversion, SDEdit, and DiffuseVAE.
- In Figure 7, the samples look like "super-resolved" VAE samples, i.e. the blurry artifacts in VAE are still maintained. Also in the second row the shape of the faces changes a lot, I cannot conclude "other stochasticities are controlled" from this result.
- More quantitative evaluations would be useful for readers to access the effectiveness of the proposed methods, e.g. CLIP score, user study etc.
- Minor issues:
	- Sec 4.1 "Since Stable Diffusion does not support resolutions other than 512 × 512", this is not true.
	- The background part is a little too long and can be shortened. Both Sec 2 and 3.1 are repeating previous works (DDPM and Textual-Inversion).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The paper is clearly written.
- My major concern is the novelty seems a little bit limited.
content.summary_of_the_review: My major concern is the novelty seems a little bit limited. Also, more evaluation and comparison is needed for readers to assess the proposed method. I might amend my score if my concerns are addressed.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this submission a method for fine-tuning large-scale text-to-image models on small datasets is presented. In order to achieve this, the method defines an optimization problem in the semantic latent space of the diffusion model. In addition, the authors also propose to use an informative initialization of the forward process to guide the pre-trained diffusion model. Experiments show that the approach outperforms the baselines both qualitatively and quantitatively with accelerated sampling speed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

- The problem is interesting to the community and has a lot of potential impact for the area of generative modeling.
- The approach makes sense and the empirical results supports the proposed contribution. 

Weaknesses:
- The paper is a bit difficult to understand. In particular is unclear what the experimental setting is. Is a single text prompt v* optimized for jointly for all the images in the dataset? If so, how does one define an initial distribution? 

- Figures 2 and 4 are hard to understand. These are not standard benchmarks, so I suggest also showing real samples from each dataset right next to the generated samples.

- The empirical evaluation is rather small. In order to understand the true empirical value of this contribution it would be good to see results using FID, SwaV-FID and IS scores. In addition to using other pre-trained models (other than stable diffusion).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- Clarity: parts of the paper and figures are not clear to this reviewer (see weaknesses). 
- Novelty: the proposed approach is a mix of two existing approaches. One for optimization (Gal et. al, 2022) and then using a VAE.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed a method for fine tuning a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model to a small dataset. The problem of fine-tuning large generative models is interesting and deserves some exposure. The proposed approach is a combination of two existing methods (Gal et. all, 2022 and VAEs). The empirical evaluation is rather small and it makes it hard to understand the true value of the proposed approach.

content.title: CUSTOMIZING PRE-TRAINED DIFFUSION MODELS FOR YOUR OWN DATA
content.TL;DR: We propose a method to utilize the pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models to generate a custom dataset.
content.abstract: Recently, several large-scale text-to-image diffusion models have been released, showing unprecedented performance. Since the shift from learning a task-specific model from scratch to leveraging pre-trained large-scale models is an inevitable trend in deep generative modeling, it is necessary to develop  methods to better utilize these models. In this paper, we propose a method dubbed Diffusion model for Your Own Data (DYOD) that can effectively utilize a pre-trained text-to-image diffusion model to approximate the implicit distribution of a custom dataset. Specifically, we first obtain a  text prompt that can best represent the custom dataset through optimization in the semantic latent space of the diffusion model. In order to be able to better control generative image content, in particular geometry of the objects, we show that the text prompt alone is not sufficient, but rather an informative initialization that can guide the pre-trained diffusion model is necessary. As representative examples, we demonstrate that  learned distribution initialization from user's data set or an image initialization by user's sketch, photo, etc. serves the goal for customizing diffusion model for user's own data. Experiments show that the customized DYOD outperforms the Stable Diffusion baselines both qualitatively and quantitatively with accelerated sampling speed.
